paras: The threatened lynching of Woodbury took place in early April 1882 on the 'big ditch' near Fort Collins, Colorado, where workers who suspected an under foreman named Woodbury of being a United States detective readied a rope to hang him. Woodbury left unharmed, and the owner of the ditch discharged the men. The only known report, a short local note in the Cheyenne Daily Leader, gives no race for anyone involved.

According to the Cheyenne Daily Leader, 'some of the men' working on the ditch came to suspect that Woodbury, an under foreman, was a federal detective 'spotting deserters'. As the feeling against him grew, they ordered him to leave. When he refused, they 'produced a rope and made ready to lynch him', and at that point he left. The paper dated the incident only to 'the other day' before its 13 April issue and named none of the men.
The men were afterward discharged by Carter-Cotton, described as the owner of the ditch. No report of arrests or of any legal action against the workers appears in the coverage.

The Cheyenne Daily Leader ran the story without a headline on 13 April 1882, among local notes on a church project, a stolen pair of boots and the weather. Its tone was light: the paragraph opened 'There might have been a lynching' and closed with the curt line 'Then he left.' No other paper is known to have carried the item.
